newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to mull de-listing saccharin as cancer risk.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to mull de-listing saccharin as cancer risk.

text.p: A U.S. health panel said on Friday it would review data that could lead to removal of the artificial sweetener saccharin from a federal list of possible carcinogens.
Saccharin has been listed as an "anticipated" carcinogen since 1981, based on evidence that included animal tests. The Calorie Control Council, an industry group, asked for the new review.

In its announcement, the National Toxicology Programme said it would examine the data under revised criteria and review procedures put in place last year by the Health and Human Services Department. The guidelines broadened the criteria for reviews and allow petitions to de-list substances.
The Food and Drug Administration took steps to partially ban saccharin in 1977, based on a Canadian study on rats. Congress intervened to allow continued sales as long as a warning label was used.
Other countries also have allowed the sale of saccharin and often, like the United States, required an advisory label.

Saccharin, discovered in 1879, is 200 to 500 times sweeter than cane sugar and sweetens foods and beverages without the calories of sugar. Aspartame and other artificial, low-calorie sweeteners have emerged in recent years as competitors of saccharin.

In the studies that led to FDA's proposed ban, rats showed a higher incidence of bladder cancer when they were fed levels of sachharin equal to 5 percent to 7.5 percent of their diet. Later studies found no increase in bladder cancer in people who consumed saccharin.
The National Toxicology Programme also said it would review several substances for possible inclusion on its list of cancer-causing substances.

The substances to be reviewed include snuff and chewing tobacco, tobacco smoke as a whole, ultraviolet radiation, whether from the sun or tanning machines, and sulphuric acid mist, which is used in making products from rayon to paper, rubber and steel. Some individual chemicals in tobacco smoke already are listed.
